paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately a Transformer can represent relationships within sequences. Its focus is a restricted architecture: a single layer with one attention head. The question concerns approximation capability, meaning how well the architecture can express a target relationship, rather than how successfully a particular training procedure will discover that representation.

The authors consider general nonlinear relationships and introduce complexity measures used to derive an explicit approximation-rate estimate. Their result is described as Jackson-type: it connects approximation accuracy with properties of the relationship being approximated. This makes the analysis more informative than a statement that an architecture can represent a relationship sufficiently well in principle.

The resulting rate reveals structural properties of the Transformer and suggests which sequential relationships it is especially suited to approximate. It also enables concrete comparisons with classical sequence models, including recurrent neural networks. The contribution is therefore a mathematical account of architectural differences within the single-layer, single-head setting studied, rather than a universal ranking of sequence-model performance.
neurips-2024-approximation-rate-of-the-t.tldr: An approximation-rate analysis explains which sequence relationships a single-layer, single-head Transformer is suited to represent.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to detect whether someone updates beliefs appropriately after receiving evidence or remains overly attached to an earlier belief. It formalizes this attachment through a specific model: a biased posterior is a weighted mixture of the original prior and the Bayesian posterior. Greater bias places more weight on the original belief.

Because beliefs may be unobservable, the proposed approach works through actions. The investigator designs signals, observes the agent's responses, and uses those responses to detect bias. This reasoning assumes that the agent chooses actions to maximize their own expected utility. Signal design therefore matters because evidence must produce behavior that reveals differences between the modeled belief updates.

The objective is to detect bias using as few signals as possible. The authors characterize circumstances in which one signal is sufficient and provide a computationally efficient algorithm for finding optimal signaling schemes. These results make detection an information-design problem with explicit assumptions, rather than treating any reluctance to change behavior as evidence of biased reasoning.
neurips-2024-bias-detection-via-signalin.tldr: Carefully designed signals can reveal attachment to prior beliefs through an agent's actions under a specified belief-update model.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a scene from only a few images leaves limited information for generating new viewpoints. Some Gaussian splatting approaches supplement those images with predictions from pretrained two-dimensional models, such as depth estimates. This paper identifies noisy and blurry predictions as a problem because they can provide imprecise guidance for learning the scene.

The proposed method instead draws supervision from binocular consistency. It constructs pairs of binocular images using disparity-guided image warping and uses agreement between those paired views as a learning signal. The central idea is that relationships between views can help constrain the reconstructed scene without requiring an external prior as supervision.

The method also constrains Gaussian opacity to regularize Gaussian locations and avoid redundant Gaussians, supporting robustness and efficiency when observations are sparse. Experiments on LLFF, DTU, and Blender report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Together, the components show how view consistency and control of the Gaussian representation can support sparse-view synthesis without the external supervision used by the approaches discussed.
neurips-2024-binocular-guided-3d-gaussia.tldr: Binocular consistency and opacity constraints improve sparse-view Gaussian splatting without external priors as supervision.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether changing the training distribution can improve performance on the original data distribution. Its starting point is simplicity bias: optimization can favor some features early instead of learning different features evenly. The authors compare gradient descent with sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, to understand how that tendency depends on the training method.

For a two-layer convolutional network, they prove that SAM learns different features more uniformly, especially early in training. They also show that examples constraining early-learned features can be separated using network outputs. Their method, USEFUL, clusters examples by early outputs, identifies a cluster with similar outputs, and upsamples the remaining examples once.

Empirically, this one-time redistribution improves generalization on the original distribution across gradient methods, including stochastic gradient descent and SAM. Combined with SAM variants and data augmentation, it achieves what the authors describe as state-of-the-art results for several named network and dataset combinations. The theoretical analysis motivates the sampling strategy, while experiments establish its usefulness across broader training configurations.
neurips-2024-changing-the-training-data-.tldr: USEFUL resamples training examples using early network outputs to reduce simplicity bias and improve generalization on the original distribution.

paragraphs: Neural causal models use generative networks constrained by a causal graph to estimate causal effects or bounds on those effects. Partial identification concerns the latter situation, where the available constraints support a range rather than a single answer. This paper asks whether neural estimates of those bounds are formally consistent as the available data grows.

Earlier consistency results covered discrete variables or linear causal models. The authors extend the analysis to a general setting containing both continuous and categorical variables. Their proof connects the ability of neural generative models to approximate structural causal models with sample complexity, then follows how those errors affect the constrained optimization defining the causal bounds.

The results show that network depth, connectivity, and Lipschitz regularization matter for consistency. A counterexample demonstrates that without this regularization, the method may fail to become consistent even asymptotically. The contribution therefore includes both a broader theoretical guarantee and a concrete reason to treat architecture and training regularization as part of the causal estimation method.
neurips-2024-consistency-of-neural-causa.tldr: The paper proves neural causal partial-identification consistency in a broader setting and shows why architecture and Lipschitz regularization matter.

paragraphs: This paper develops a diffusion architecture that learns image generation and segmentation together without region annotations. Training uses only the denoising diffusion objective, so the segmentation behavior must arise from how the network solves its generation task. The model receives no prior knowledge about image regions during training.

The key intervention is a computational bottleneck built into the architecture. It encourages the network to partition an image into regions, denoise those regions in parallel, and combine their outputs. Because predicted partitions are part of this internal computation, examining them provides semantic segmentations of the synthetic images the trained model generates.

The same trained model can also segment real images without additional fine-tuning. It first adds noise to a real image and then denoises it, exposing partitions through that process. Experiments across multiple datasets report accurate unsupervised segmentation alongside high-quality generation. The approach makes segmentation an outcome of an architectural constraint within generative learning, allowing one training objective to support both tasks.
neurips-2024-factorized-diffusion-archit.tldr: A region-based computational bottleneck lets a diffusion model learn image generation and segmentation using only denoising supervision.

paragraphs: Few-shot diffusion adapts a pretrained generator to a user-defined concept using limited target examples. This paper analyzes why pretraining can make that adaptation effective under a linear distribution structure with latent dimension d. It separates the contribution of source samples, n_s, from the contribution of target samples, n_ta.

For target-score approximation, the authors prove a bound of order n_s^(-2/d) + n_ta^(-1/2), up to logarithmic factors. Compared with the cited n_ta^(-2/d) result, this separates the dimension-dependent source term from a target term whose exponent does not depend on d. In a latent Gaussian special case, they also derive a closed-form optimizer and an empirical-solution accuracy bound of order 1/n_ta + 1/sqrt(n_s), again up to logarithmic factors.

Real-world experiments further show that tuning only the encoder and decoder specific to the target distribution can generate new images carrying the target feature. Those observations support the theoretical account. The stated structural assumptions remain central: the analysis explains favorable target-sample dependence in the modeled setting, rather than establishing dimension-independent adaptation for every diffusion problem.
neurips-2024-few-shot-diffusion-models-e.tldr: Under a linear latent structure, few-shot diffusion has favorable target-sample error bounds that help explain efficient adaptation.

paragraphs: FlashAttention-3 targets the attention computation that can bottleneck large language models and long-context applications. Earlier attention acceleration reduced memory traffic, but the abstract reports that FlashAttention-2 used only 35% of H100 GPU capacity. This work seeks additional performance by organizing computation around capabilities of Hopper GPUs.

Two techniques exploit asynchronous execution. Warp specialization overlaps computation with data movement, while another scheduling strategy interleaves blockwise matrix multiplication and softmax. A third technique combines block quantization with incoherent processing to use FP8 hardware. These changes address both keeping hardware busy and carrying out attention efficiently at lower numerical precision.

On H100 GPUs, the authors report speedups of 1.5–2.0 times, with BF16 reaching up to 840 TFLOPs/s and 85% utilization. FP8 reaches 1.3 PFLOPs/s, and its numerical error is reported as 2.6 times lower than a baseline FP8 attention implementation. The findings demonstrate gains for the attention operation on the evaluated hardware, combining higher throughput with improved accuracy relative to that low-precision baseline.
neurips-2024-flashattention-3-fast-and-a.tldr: FlashAttention-3 accelerates attention on Hopper GPUs through asynchronous scheduling and FP8 processing with improved numerical accuracy.

paragraphs: Extracting blood vessels or road networks requires recovering how branches connect, as well as identifying the pixels they occupy. GraphMorph approaches this through branch-level features. Its purpose is to produce predictions with more accurate topology by explicitly representing the tubular structure as a graph within each image patch.

A Graph Decoder takes features at multiple scales from a segmentation network and predicts that graph. A separate Morph Module then combines the graph with the network's centerline probability map. Using the proposed SkeletonDijkstra algorithm, it creates a centerline mask aligned with the predicted graph, linking the branch representation to an image-based output.

The authors also use GraphMorph's centerline masks in a simple post-processing strategy for segmentation. They observe a significant reduction in false positives, showing that the structural prediction can improve the broader segmentation result as well as centerline extraction. Evaluations across multiple datasets support both uses. The method's central contribution is a connection between learned branch structure and the final centerline mask.
neurips-2024-graphmorph-tubular-structur.tldr: GraphMorph predicts branch graphs and converts them into centerline masks to improve tubular topology and reduce segmentation false positives.

paragraphs: Efficient fine-tuning aims to adapt large pretrained networks with a manageable number of trainable parameters. This paper works within orthogonal fine-tuning, which adapts pretrained weights using orthogonal matrices. Its central question is how to represent those transformations more economically while preserving the orthogonal structure required by the approach.

The authors introduce a class of structured matrices that encompasses and generalizes classes from earlier work. They study its properties and use it to build a structured orthogonal parameterization. Incorporating that parameterization into the fine-tuning framework improves parameter efficiency, making the representation of the adaptation itself the main point of intervention.

Empirical evaluations cover text-to-image diffusion model adaptation and downstream language-model fine-tuning. The authors also extend the construction to orthogonal convolutions and experiment with 1-Lipschitz neural networks. These applications show the construction being used beyond one model family or task. The stated contribution combines a general matrix framework with practical adaptations, rather than presenting an efficiency technique tied solely to one particular pretrained network.
neurips-2024-group-and-shuffle-efficient.tldr: A generalized structured-matrix construction makes orthogonal fine-tuning more parameter-efficient and extends to orthogonal convolutions.

paragraphs: HDR-GS generates new views of a scene while representing a wider brightness range than ordinary low-dynamic-range images. It addresses the training and rendering costs of existing NeRF-based HDR approaches. The framework produces HDR views and can also reconstruct LDR images at an exposure time chosen by the user.

Its scene representation is a Gaussian point cloud supporting both brightness ranges. Spherical harmonics fit HDR color, while a neural tone-mapper produces LDR color. Two parallel differentiable rasterization processes turn these colors into the respective images. The authors also recalibrate camera parameters and compute initial Gaussian positions to establish a data foundation for this approach.

Experiments report improvements of 3.84 dB for LDR and 1.91 dB for HDR novel-view synthesis over the state-of-the-art NeRF-based comparison. They also report 1000 times the inference speed while using 6.3% of the training time. These results indicate that, in the evaluated setting, the dual-range Gaussian representation improves rendering quality while substantially reducing the cost of learning and displaying new views.
neurips-2024-hdr-gs-efficient-high-dynam.tldr: HDR-GS uses a dual-range Gaussian scene representation to improve HDR and LDR view synthesis while greatly reducing reported training and rendering costs.

paragraphs: Instruction tuning commonly focuses its training loss on the model's response. This paper proposes Instruction Modelling, which also applies loss to the instruction and prompt portions of the training material. The change makes those portions participate directly in learning instead of using them solely as the context for predicting an answer.

Across 21 benchmarks, the authors find improvements in many settings, covering NLP tasks and open-ended generation. The largest reported case more than doubles performance on AlpacaEval 1.0. Effectiveness depends on the ratio of instruction length to output length and the number of training examples, so the reported benefit is sensitive to the training data.

The method is especially beneficial with long instructions and short responses, or when instruction tuning uses few examples. Further analysis supports the authors' hypothesis that reduced overfitting contributes to the gains. They present the work as practical guidance for instruction tuning, particularly under limited resources, rather than as a replacement for the existing tuning process.
neurips-2024-instruction-tuning-with-los.tldr: Including instructions and prompts in the training loss can improve instruction tuning, particularly with few examples or long instructions and short answers.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly evaluate text, including their own responses. This paper investigates self-preference: a model gives its own output a higher score even when human annotators judge competing outputs equally good. The authors ask whether this bias is connected to an ability to recognize which text the model itself produced.

They find that models including GPT-4 and Llama 2 have nontrivial self-recognition accuracy without additional training, distinguishing their outputs from those of other models and humans. Fine-tuning experiments reveal a linear correlation between self-recognition capability and self-preference strength. Controlled experiments further show that a causal explanation withstands straightforward confounding explanations.

The findings identify self-recognition as a potential contributor to biased evaluation, with implications for benchmarking, reward modeling, and self-refinement. A stronger preference for a model's own response may therefore reflect something beyond the response quality humans perceive. The paper connects a capability to an evaluation bias while keeping the evidence grounded in the models and experimental manipulations studied.
neurips-2024-llm-evaluators-recognize-an.tldr: Experiments connect language models' ability to recognize their own outputs with a tendency to favor those outputs when evaluating quality.

paragraphs: A language model can answer equivalent requests very differently depending on their wording. This paper introduces RobustAlpacaEval to examine that sensitivity at the level of individual user queries. It emphasizes the weakest performance among equivalent prompts as a way to assess how unreliable an otherwise capable model's responses can become.

The benchmark evaluates ChatGPT and six open-source models from the Llama, Mistral, and Gemma families. The authors report substantial variation: Llama-2-70B-chat has a reported 45.48% difference between its best and worst performance, with the latter reaching 9.38%. This shifts attention from successful wording to the range of outcomes available under meaning-preserving changes.

The study also investigates how to locate weak prompts using approaches with and without model-specific information, finding no straightforward shortcut in its analysis. Existing prompt engineering and prompt consistency methods provide limited improvement to worst-prompt performance. The results motivate evaluating resilience across varied user phrasing, because good performance under selected prompts can coexist with much weaker performance under equivalent requests.
neurips-2024-on-the-worst-prompt-perform.tldr: RobustAlpacaEval reveals large performance drops across equivalent user queries and limited gains from existing prompt-robustness methods.

paragraphs: Predicting systems governed by partial differential equations can be expensive when numerical methods need fine spatial grids and small time steps. P²C²Net aims to make these predictions on coarser grids with limited training data. It combines a numerical update structure with learned corrections, embedding the governing equations into the model.

A trainable PDE block updates the system state using a high-order numerical scheme with encoded boundary conditions. A neural block corrects the solution as prediction proceeds. The model also uses a learnable symmetric convolutional filter, shared throughout the architecture, to estimate spatial derivatives from the corrected state. This links the learned corrections back into subsequent equation-based updates.

The authors report accurate accelerated predictions with training data as limited as three to five trajectories. Across four datasets involving reaction-diffusion processes and turbulent flows, they report consistent state-of-the-art performance with gains exceeding 50%, including in relative prediction error. The results support combining numerical structure and ongoing neural correction to make coarse-grid prediction effective in the evaluated small-data settings.
neurips-2024-p-2-c-2-net-pde-preserved-c.tldr: P²C²Net combines equation-based updates with neural corrections for accurate, efficient coarse-grid dynamics prediction from limited training trajectories.

paragraphs: Two-sided matching connects participants from opposite sides of a market according to their preferences. In applications such as online labor or content matching, one side may initially lack knowledge of its own preferences over the other. This paper studies how learning those preferences affects the ability to produce a stable final matching.

The authors focus on stability, a game-theoretic property that receives less attention in prior online work centered on welfare and regret. They use the structure of stable solutions to design algorithms that increase the likelihood of finding them. Their theoretical analysis bounds how many samples are needed to reach a stable matching with high probability.

Experiments reveal tradeoffs between stability and optimality for the proposed algorithms, complementing the sample-complexity results. This distinction matters because improving an aggregate performance objective does not by itself settle whether the final matching has the desired stability property. The contribution treats learning effort and matching stability together, providing probabilistic guarantees rather than assuming preferences are already known.
neurips-2024-putting-gale-shapley-to-wor.tldr: The paper designs learning algorithms and sample-complexity bounds for reaching stable matchings with high probability when preferences are initially unknown.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing offers a low-cost way to update incorrect or outdated information in a language model, but edited models can lose performance. This paper investigates that degradation from two directions: properties of the editing data and properties of the model layers being changed. It then uses the findings to motivate an editing method.

For the data analysis, the authors construct the Multi-Question Dataset to compare different types of editing examples. Their experiments identify editing-target diversity and sequence length as major influences on performance. On the model side, they find a strong correlation between the editing layer's L1 norm and editing accuracy, identifying that quantity as an important factor in the observed bottleneck.

The proposed Dump for Sequence method, D4S, reduces the editing layer's L1 norm. The authors report that this overcomes the previous bottleneck, supports multiple effective edits, and minimizes damage to the model. The work connects an empirical diagnosis of editing degradation with a targeted intervention, while also showing that the composition of editing data matters.
neurips-2024-reasons-and-solutions-for-t.tldr: D4S reduces an editing layer's L1 norm to support repeated knowledge edits with less model damage, following analyses of data and model factors.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across clients without sharing their raw data, but repeatedly exchanging models can be costly. One-shot federated learning reduces that communication to a single round, often sacrificing accuracy when clients have different data distributions. Fens explores a middle ground through an ensemble of locally trained models.

Clients first train their own models and send them to the server, as in one-shot learning. They then collaboratively train a lightweight prediction aggregator using federated learning. This second phase learns how to combine the models' predictions while concentrating additional communication on a small aggregation model. Fens therefore includes communication beyond the initial one-shot exchange.

Across experiments with different datasets and heterogeneity levels, Fens approaches conventional federated accuracy. For heterogeneous CIFAR-10, the abstract reports up to 26.9% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art one-shot methods and accuracy only 3.1% below federated learning. Fens uses at most 4.3 times one-shot communication, while conventional federated learning uses at least 10.9 times more communication than Fens in the reported comparisons.
neurips-2024-revisiting-ensembling-in-on.tldr: Fens combines locally trained models through a lightweight federated aggregator, improving the accuracy–communication tradeoff over one-shot learning.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether safety benchmark improvements distinguish safety progress from broader increases in model capability. Its starting observation is that performance on many machine-learning benchmarks correlates strongly with model scale. If safety scores follow the same underlying pattern, their improvement may be difficult to interpret as a distinct safety advance.

The authors use spectral analysis to extract a capabilities component from benchmark results. This component is the direction across benchmark scores that explains the greatest variation in model performance. They then examine existing safety benchmarks and find that this shared component explains much of the performance variation on many of them.

Based on that analysis, the authors argue for prioritizing safety metrics that are not highly correlated with scale. Their method provides a way to scrutinize both new benchmarks and proposed safety methods for progress distinguishable from general capability gains. The finding concerns many evaluated benchmarks; it does not establish that every safety measure is merely a capability test.
neurips-2024-safetywashing-do-ai-safety-.tldr: Spectral analysis finds that general capabilities explain much of the variation on many safety benchmarks, complicating claims of distinct safety progress.

paragraphs: Stormer is a weather forecasting model built with minimal changes to a standard Transformer. The paper responds to a difficulty in interpreting earlier systems: complex customized architectures can make it unclear which components drive success. The authors use empirical analyses to identify useful elements, including weather-specific embeddings, a randomized forecasting objective, and pressure-weighted loss.

The central training objective asks the model to predict weather dynamics over varying time intervals. At inference, this supports producing multiple forecasts for the same target lead time and combining them to improve accuracy. Learning across different intervals therefore contributes directly to how the model constructs its final forecast.

On WeatherBench 2, Stormer is competitive at short and medium ranges and outperforms current methods beyond seven days, while using orders of magnitude less training data and compute. The authors also observe consistent accuracy improvements as model size and training tokens increase. These findings support both the selected forecasting components and the scaling potential of the relatively simple architecture.
neurips-2024-scaling-transformer-neural-.tldr: Stormer combines a minimally modified Transformer with variable-interval forecasting to achieve strong weather predictions and favorable scaling.

paragraphs: This paper develops SDEPO, a natural policy gradient algorithm for two-player zero-sum Markov games. The theoretical setting allows continuously varying states but finitely many actions. The goal is to learn strategies approaching a Nash equilibrium, with a convergence guarantee that does not depend on counting the states in that continuous space.

During policy evaluation, a kernel embedding constructs a finite-dimensional linear approximation of the state-action value function. The authors explicitly account for the error introduced by this approximation. They prove last-iterate convergence to an epsilon-optimal equilibrium with complexity of order 1/((1−gamma)^3 epsilon), up to logarithmic factors, where gamma is the discount factor.

The stated complexity matches the best-known global convergence results for policy gradient algorithms in the single-agent setting. The paper also introduces a practical variant for continuous actions and reports empirical superiority. These are distinct contributions: the finite-action analysis supplies the formal guarantee, while the continuous-action variant extends the method's practical scope through experimental evaluation.
neurips-2024-solving-zero-sum-markov-gam.tldr: SDEPO uses finite-dimensional kernel embeddings to obtain state-cardinality-independent convergence guarantees for continuous-state, finite-action zero-sum games.

paragraphs: SpatialPIN addresses spatial reasoning in vision-language models, with an emphasis on tasks that require understanding a three-dimensional scene. The authors argue that success on spatial visual question answering may not provide the explicit 3D understanding needed for higher-level tasks such as describing dynamic scene changes or planning motion.

The framework enhances a vision-language model through prompting and interaction with priors from multiple 3D foundation models. It operates in a zero-shot, training-free manner, so the proposed enhancement comes from using those existing models and their information during interaction. This makes explicit 3D information a central part of the framework's approach to spatial reasoning.

Experiments show good performance across different forms of spatial visual question answering. The authors also demonstrate that the enhanced model can help with downstream robotics tasks, including picking and stacking objects and trajectory planning. These findings support extending the framework beyond answering spatial questions to assisting tasks that involve action, while the claim remains one of demonstrated assistance in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-spatialpin-enhancing-spatia.tldr: SpatialPIN uses prompting and existing 3D model priors to improve spatial reasoning and assist robotics tasks without additional training.

paragraphs: Zero-shot node classification assigns graph nodes to classes that were absent during training. A central difficulty is prediction bias: nodes from unseen classes are incorrectly assigned to familiar classes. SpeAr addresses this by making greater use of cluster structure within unlabeled nodes, alongside learnable representations of the classes.

The authors establish an approximate relationship between minimizing a spectral contrastive loss and performing spectral decomposition of the graph. This provides a basis for learning node representations through loss minimization while capturing implicit graph clusters. Class prototypes start from semantic vectors and are then iteratively refined using the learned node representations.

The approach links two sources of information: semantic initialization for the classes and structural evidence from the graph. Refinement allows the class representatives to respond to the node representations rather than remaining fixed at initialization. Extensive experiments support the method's effectiveness and show that it can further alleviate prediction bias. The result is a method for reducing the unseen-to-seen misclassification tendency, rather than a claim that the bias disappears entirely.
neurips-2024-spear-a-spectral-approach-f.tldr: SpeAr combines spectral graph learning with refined class prototypes to reduce bias against unseen classes in zero-shot node classification.

paragraphs: Capability evaluations can underestimate a language model when ordinary prompts fail to expose what it can do. This paper constructs password-locked models to test elicitation methods under controlled concealment. These models are trained to show particular capabilities when a password appears and otherwise imitate a substantially weaker model.

The test is whether further training can recover those capabilities without the password. The authors find that a few high-quality demonstrations are often enough for full elicitation. Fine-tuning can also reveal other capabilities locked behind the same password or even different passwords. When demonstrations are unavailable but evaluations exist, reinforcement-learning approaches are still often successful.

These findings support fine-tuning as an effective elicitation method for hidden capabilities in current models, while preserving an important qualification. Elicitation may be unreliable without high-quality demonstrations, including when the concealed capability exceeds what human demonstrators can show. The password setup provides a way to test recovery of deliberately hidden abilities and examine the conditions under which the recovery succeeds.
neurips-2024-stress-testing-capability-e.tldr: Password-locked models show that fine-tuning often reveals hidden capabilities, but elicitation may be unreliable without high-quality demonstrations.

paragraphs: Spry targets the memory burden of federated language-model fine-tuning on constrained devices. Backpropagation stores intermediate activations, while forward-mode automatic differentiation can reduce that storage. Directly using forward mode, however, produces slow convergence and poor accuracy in the authors' observations. Spry divides trainable weights among clients to obtain closer gradient estimates.

The analysis proves that global gradient estimates are unbiased when clients have homogeneous data distributions. Heterogeneity increases their bias, and the convergence result reflects that restriction: gradients decrease inversely with the number of federated rounds, up to limits imposed by heterogeneity. The guarantee therefore depends on how data differs across participating clients.

Experiments report 1.4–7.1 times lower training memory than backpropagation with comparable accuracy. Against state-of-the-art zero-order methods, Spry reduces convergence time by factors of 1.2–20.3 and reports 5.2–13.5% higher accuracy. For Llama2-7B with LoRA, peak memory falls from 33.9 GB to 6.2 GB. These results show how distributing the gradient-computation burden can expand feasible federated deployments.
neurips-2024-thinking-forward-memory-eff.tldr: Spry distributes trainable weights across clients to make forward-mode federated fine-tuning more memory-efficient, with convergence affected by data heterogeneity.
